## Core Concept
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="ArticleMedia" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: id="media-lea-strc-001-05-core-concept", type="image", caption="Internal Forces — Tension, Compression, Shear, Bending, and Torsion", description="Five-panel illustration showing each internal force type: (1) Tension — pulling arrows elongating a member; (2) Compression — pushing arrows shortening a member with buckling indicator; (3) Shear — transverse sliding action at a cut section; (4) Bending — curved member showing compression/tension faces; (5) Torsion — twisting moment about longitudinal axis. Each panel shows the force direction, member deformation, and a real structural example.", suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image", status="placeholder"
- Text: (none detected)
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

When loads are applied to a structure, they cause internal forces to develop within the structural members. Cutting a member at any cross-section and examining the internal actions reveals forces and moments that keep the separated portions in equilibrium. Five types of internal forces are fundamental to structural behavior:

**Tension (T):**
A pulling force that acts along the longitudinal axis of a member, pulling the two cut sections apart. The fibers of the member are being stretched. Example: Cables in a suspension bridge, the lower chord of a truss, steel rods in a tie-down system. Under tension, the member tries to elongate.

**Compression (C):**
A pushing force that acts along the longitudinal axis, pushing the two cut sections together. The fibers are being squeezed. Example: Columns supporting a building, the upper chord of a truss, studs in a wall frame. Under compression, the member tries to shorten. Compression is critical because it can lead to buckling if the member is slender.

**Shear (V):**
A force that acts perpendicular (transverse) to the longitudinal axis of the member, tending to slide one portion past the adjacent portion. If two halves of a member are cut by a horizontal plane and one half tends to move up or down relative to the other, shear is present. Example: A beam loaded perpendicular to its length develops shear. Shear forces create a sliding tendency; large shear can cause the member to split along the grain (in timber) or fail by diagonal cracking (in concrete).

**Bending (Moment, M):**
A couple (moment) that acts to bend or flex the member. Bending causes one face to be in compression and the opposite face to be in tension along the length of the member. A pure bending moment has no net force but creates rotation and curvature. Example: Any loaded beam experiences bending. The upper fibers may be in compression (curved downward); the lower fibers in tension (stretched). Bending causes flexural stress that varies across the section.

**Torsion (T or τ):**
A twisting moment that acts about the longitudinal axis, causing the member to rotate or twist. Torsion develops when loads are applied off-center or when a member is twisted by external forces. Example: A drive shaft, a beam with eccentric loading, a building corner with asymmetric load paths. Torsion causes shear stress on the surface of the member; the interior experiences lower stress.

Each internal force type has distinct causes and effects on the structure. Tension and compression are axial; shear is transverse; bending and torsion are moments. A structural member may experience more than one type simultaneously (e.g., a loaded beam experiences both shear and bending).

## Key Provisions

| Internal Force | Direction | Effect | Symbol | Typical Location |
|---|----------|--------|--------|------------|
| **Tension** | Axial (pulling) | Elongation; fiber stretching | T | Cable members; ties; lower chord truss |
| **Compression** | Axial (pushing) | Shortening; fiber squeezing; buckling risk | C | Columns; upper chord truss; studs |
| **Shear** | Transverse (perpendicular to length) | Sliding tendency; diagonal cracking (concrete); grain splitting (timber) | V | Beam ends; near supports |
| **Bending** | Moment; perpendicular load | Curvature; compression on one face, tension on opposite | M | Loaded beams; span center (positive M), supports (negative M) |
| **Torsion** | Moment; about longitudinal axis | Twisting; shear stress on member surface | T or τ | Eccentric loading; skew structures; drive shafts |

## Shear as an Internal Force Concept

Shear (V) is the internal force concept owned here. Shear represents the internal action at a section that prevents one portion of the member from sliding past the adjacent portion. In a loaded beam, shear force is highest at the supports and decreases toward midspan. The magnitude and direction of shear at any section must be determined by free-body diagram equilibrium; shear values are not assigned arbitrarily.

**Note:** Shear strength formulas (e.g., timber shear formula 3V/2A) and stress/strain relationships are covered in other articles and are NOT part of this topic. Similarly, stress calculations and material-specific shear capacity checks are separate.

## Philippine Practice Context

In Philippine structural design, engineers identify internal forces through free-body diagrams and load path tracing. Reinforced concrete design accounts for tension (longitudinal steel), compression (concrete), shear (stirrups), and bending (flexure). Steel design manages tension (plates, welds), compression (buckling of columns and plate elements), shear (bolts, welds), bending (beam sections), and torsion (corner braces). Timber design addresses compression (parallel to grain), tension (perpendicular grain splitting), shear (grain splitting), bending (MOE checks), and torsion (less common but present in skew structures).

## How It's Tested

1. **Identification:** "At the support of a loaded beam, which internal force is typically largest?" — tests understanding of shear distribution.
2. **Effect Matching:** "Which internal force causes one face of a beam to go into compression and the opposite face into tension?" — tests bending concept.
3. **Cause and Effect:** "A beam with off-center loading develops what type of internal force?" — tests torsion understanding.
4. **Conceptual Application:** "In a cable-supported structure, the cables experience primarily ___." — tests tension concept application.

See also: **Force Properties** (lea-strc-001-01) for the fundamentals, **Beam Types** (lea-strc-001-04) for where internal forces develop, and **Stress** (lea-strc-003-01) for how internal forces translate to material stress.

## Common Mistakes

A beam can have shear with zero moment at one section and moment with zero shear at another.\",\"Confusing torsion with bending: Torsion twists the member about its axis; bending curves it perpendicular to the axis. A twisted beam and a bent beam have opposite failure modes.\",\"Assuming all axial force is tension: Compression is equally important; columns are critical structural elements that must be designed for compressive strength and buckling resistance. Compression is not a weakness; it is a load type.\",\"Forgetting that tension cannot reverse in some materials: Concrete and masonry have low or zero tensile strength. ## Learning Goal
Design parking structure geometry — ramp grades (max 1:7), bay widths, aisle dimensions, column spacing, and turning radii — to accommodate vehicle maneuverability, verify accessible stall dimensions (3.7m × 5.0m), and apply structural and operational constraints.

Parking structure geometry—ramp grades, bay widths, aisle dimensions, column spacing, and turning radii—determines whether a parking design is buildable and user-friendly. 
## Core Concept

A parking structure must accommodate vehicle maneuverability, emergency egress, and structural efficiency. The geometry is constrained by:

1. **Vehicle envelope:** Standard car (2.5m × 5.0m) turning radius ~6.1m (inside wheel).
2. **Ramp gradient:** Strictly limited to **1:6 (16.7%)** maximum for vehicles.
3. **Bay layout:** Angle of parking (90°, 60°, 45°) determines the required aisle width.
4. **Vertical clearance:** Minimum **2.40 m** for standard vehicle areas; **2.20 m** minimum for accessible pedestrian walkways and signage per BP 344 2024.
5. **Column grid:** Structural economics versus parking efficiency trade-off.

### Worked Example: 90° Double-Loaded Module

**Layout Parameters:**

- **Standard Stalls:** 2.5m × 5.0m.
- **Two-way Aisle:** 6.1 m (Minimum for 90° perpendicular parking).

**Calculation:**

- Stall Depth (Side A) + Aisle + Stall Depth (Side B)
- 5.0 m + 6.1 m + 5.0 m = **16.1 m** (Clear width between walls/columns).
- Structural planning typically uses an **18.5 m** module to account for structural columns and "turnplates".

**Ramp Design:**

- To rise 3.0 m (one floor level) at a **1:6 gradient**:
- $3.0\text{ m} \times 6 = 18.0\text{ m}$ total ramp length.

## Key Provisions

### Drive Aisle Widths (PD 1096 & Professional Practice)

| Parking Angle           | Traffic Flow | Minimum Aisle Width |
| :---------------------- | :----------- | :------------------ |
| **90° (Perpendicular)** | Two-Way      | **6.1 m**           |
| **90° (Perpendicular)** | One-Way      | **5.5 m**           |
| **60° (Angled)**        | One-Way      | **5.5 m**           |
| **45° (Angled)**        | One-Way      | **3.7 m**           |

### BP 344 2024 Accessibility Standards

- **Accessible Parking Slot:** **4.00 m × 5.00 m** (minimum).
- **Walkway Headroom:** **2.20 m** clear height.
- **Accessible Ramp:** **1:12** is the enforceable minimum for building permits, though **1:20** is the preferred design standard.
- **Landing:** Minimum **1.80 m** length at the top, bottom, and every 10.50 m of ramp.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Aisle Width Selection**
Question: "What is the minimum drive aisle for 90° two-way traffic?"

- **Answer:** 6.1 m.

**Pattern 2: Ramp Calculation**
Question: "A vehicle ramp must rise 4.0 m. What is the minimum length?"

- **Calculation:** $4.0 \times 6 = 24.0\text{ m}$.

**Pattern 3: Clearance Compliance**
Question: "Is a 2.10 m headroom compliant for a PWD walkway?"

- **Answer:** **No.** BP 344 2024 requires a minimum of **2.20 m**.

**Exam Tip:** Ramp grades in parking structures: max 1:7 (14.3%) per PD 1096. Bay width for 90° parking: 2.5m × 5.0m standard, 2.7m × 5.0m for compact accessible. Aisle width for 90°: 6.1m minimum.

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the task in one sentence: what concept is being identified, compared, sequenced, or applied? Then anchor your answer to the article's stated scope and avoid importing details from a different topic.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Lea Plan 008 05 Core Concept** as enough to answer. For exam practice, first identify the exact concept being asked, then choose the option that matches that concept.


## Learning Goal
Distinguish urban regeneration (large-scale redevelopment) from placemaking (incremental community activation) and tactical urbanism (low-cost temporary interventions), apply each approach to Philippine urban scenarios, and evaluate gentrification risks.

Urban regeneration and placemaking transform neglected, underutilized, or blighted urban areas into vibrant, economically productive, and culturally significant places. While urban regeneration encompasses large-scale redevelopment and infrastructure investment, placemaking emphasizes incremental, community-driven activation of public spaces and places. Tactical urbanism—low-cost, temporary interventions—serves both strategies as a rapid prototyping and community engagement tool.

## Core Concept

Urban regeneration refers to planned, systematic redevelopment of degraded urban areas to restore economic and social vitality. This may involve infrastructure investment, building rehabilitation, land assembly for new development, or institutional repositioning (e.g., converting a declining industrial area into a cultural or innovation district). Regeneration is not neutral—it always involves questions of who benefits, who is displaced, and whether existing communities are included or priced out.

Placemaking is the process of creating meaningful public spaces and experiences that strengthen community identity and social connection. Placemaking focuses on the human-scale experience: public gathering spaces, pedestrian activation, cultural events, street life. Unlike large-scale redevelopment, placemaking often works with existing conditions and emphasizes community voice.

**Tactical urbanism** encompasses low-cost, temporary interventions that test ideas or activate spaces: temporary parks (parklets), street murals, pop-up retail, community gardens, guerrilla gardening, temporary street closures for events. Tactical interventions serve two functions:

1. **Rapid prototyping** — test design ideas before major capital investment (e.g., a temporary pedestrian plaza reveals whether the location would support permanent plaza development)
2. **Community engagement** — low-risk interventions build trust and demonstrate how spaces can be improved

Adaptive reuse—converting buildings from one use to another (warehouse to lofts, church to restaurant, office to residential)—is both a regeneration strategy and a sustainability practice, preserving existing structures rather than demolishing.

## Philippine Context

Philippine cities have significant areas suitable for regeneration: aging colonial districts (Intramuros, Vigan), declining river corridors (Pasig River, Marikina River), underutilized waterfronts, and deteriorating inner-city neighborhoods. Intramuros regeneration efforts, the Port Area redevelopment in Manila, and river corridor rehabilitation projects demonstrate both the potential and the challenges. Gentrification—displacement of long-term residents and small businesses as property values rise—is a real risk in successful regeneration, particularly in informal settlement areas. Philippine planners must balance regeneration's economic benefits against community displacement through anti-displacement policies and inclusive placemaking.

## How It's Tested

1. **Tactic urbanism identification and application** — "What is tactical urbanism, and provide an example." → Answer: Low-cost, temporary interventions that test design ideas or activate spaces; examples include parklets, street murals, temporary street closures. Tests concept definition and practical understanding.

2. **Adaptive reuse concept** — "A 50-year-old warehouse in a declining district is converted to artist lofts. Is this adaptive reuse, and what planning benefit does it provide?" → Answer: Yes; it preserves the existing building (sustainable), generates economic activity and cultural vitality, and often triggers broader district regeneration. Tests understanding of both adaptive reuse definition and urban regeneration process.

3. **Displacement and community impact** — "A waterfront regeneration project transforms a degraded area into a high-value mixed-use district. What planning risk must be mitigated?" → Answer: Gentrification and displacement of original residents; mitigation requires anti-displacement policies (community land trusts, affordable housing preservation, local hiring). Tests understanding of the social risks of regeneration.

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Exam Tip:** Three key distinctions: (1) Regeneration = large-scale, top-down, capital-intensive. (2) Placemaking = community-driven, incremental, public space-focused. (3) Tactical urbanism = low-cost, temporary, rapid prototyping (pop-up bike lanes, parklets). Know which approach fits which scenario.

See **LEA-PLAN-008-03** (Sustainable Development) for sustainable regeneration, **LEA-PLAN-003-06** (Informal Settlements) for community displacement in regeneration, and **LEA-PLAN-002-06** (Urban Design) for street-level placemaking.

**Renaissance architecture** (14th–16th centuries, centered in Florence and Italy) represents a conscious *revival and reinvention* of Classical Antiquity coupled with new mathematical and humanistic thinking. Medieval Gothic gives way to rational proportions, geometric perfection, and human-scaled spaces inspired by Roman temples and Italian Renaissance humanism.


[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="ArticleMedia" status="preserved"]

The period divides into **Early Renaissance** (15th century, Florence) and **High Renaissance** (early 16th century, Rome). Early Renaissance rediscovered Classical orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian), geometric proportion, and linear perspective in architecture. High Renaissance synthesized these discoveries into monumental, spatially integrated designs.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:

- Text: **Memory Aid: Renaissance Architects.** Brunelleschi = Engineering genius (dome, perspective). Alberti = Theorist (wrote the rulebook). Bramante = Inventor of centralized plans. Michelangelo = Master of domes and spatial power. Each contributed differently; all shaped Renaissance.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Filippo Brunelleschi** (1377–1446) launched the Renaissance. His **Florence Cathedral dome** (construction 1420–1436, Florence) solved a 100-year-old engineering problem: how to vault the cathedral's 42-meter opening without a wooden centering (lost to earlier wars). Brunelleschi used a double-shell dome with internal ribbing (24 meridian ribs and 10 parallel ribs connecting the shells), creating the engineering marvel that announced the Renaissance to the world. He also studied Roman ruins, mastered mathematics, and established linear perspective in architecture (the Ospedlea degli Innocenti, 1419, demonstrates perfect geometric clarity).

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Note" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Key Clarification:** Brunelleschi's dome is both engineering *and* symbol—it announces Classical revival through its form, announces Florence's wealth and power, and demonstrates Renaissance humanistic mastery over nature. Do not separate engineering from meaning.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Leon Battista Alberti** (1404–1472) was architecture's first theorist. His *De re aedificatoria* (*On the Art of Building in Ten Books*, written 1443–1452, first printed 1485) codified Renaissance principles: proportion, harmony, human measure, and Classical orders as the basis for all design. His buildings (Palazzo Rucellai, Florence, begun 1446–completed c. 1460s; Santa Maria Novella facade, Florence, 1470; Sant'Andrea, Mantua, begun 1472–completed 1731) translate theory into practice—rational facades using Classical proportions, geometric clarity, harmonic relationships derived from musical intervals.

**Donato Bramante** (1444–1514) pioneered the **centralized Renaissance church**—a perfect geometric form (usually circular, square, or Greek cross) symbolizing divine harmony. His **Tempietto** (1502, Rome, S. Pietro in Montorio) is the Renaissance ideal distilled: a miniature circular temple with a colonnade of Doric columns, golden proportions, and Classical simplicity. Later, he designed the initial plan for **St. Peter's Basilica** (begun 1506, Rome) as a Greek cross with a central dome, establishing the model High Renaissance churches followed.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Critical Distinction:** Do not treat Brunelleschi's dome as "just" an engineering feat. The dome is both engineering *and* symbol. It announces Classical revival, announces Florence's power, and demonstrates humanistic mastery. Similarly, do not treat Bramante's centralized churches as "just" geometric games—they symbolize divine harmony and perfect order.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Michelangelo** (1475–1564) dominated High Renaissance and pioneered Mannerism. After Bramante's death, he became chief architect of St. Peter's (1547), redesigning it into a more compact Greek cross emphasizing the dome. His dome (1547–1564, completed posthumously) becomes the architectural icon of the Renaissance—a culmination of engineering (double shell like Brunelleschi's), proportion, and humanistic ambition. Michelangelo's late work shows Mannerist traits: tension, distortion of Classical rules, dramatic light-and-shadow contrasts.

**Andrea Palladio** (1508–1580) codified Renaissance villa architecture and proportion systems. His *Four Books on Architecture* (*I Quattro Libri*, 1570) systematized orders, proportions, and designs, becoming the most influential architectural treatise after Vitruvius. His villas (Villa Rotonda, Vicenza, begun 1567–completed 1590s; Villa Emo, Fanzolo, 1558–1559) use Classical temple fronts with colonnades, central rotundas with domes, and perfect geometric proportions. These designs synthesize rural functionality with Classical grandeur, establishing a model for manor houses across Europe and America for centuries.

**Renaissance principles:**
- **Human measure**: Proportion based on human body and Classical ratios
- **Geometric perfection**: Circle, square, and Greek cross as ideal forms
- **Classical orders**: Systematic use of Doric, Ionic, Corinthian columns and entablatures
- **Harmonic proportion**: Proportions derived from musical intervals (ratios like 1:1, 2:3, 3:4)
- **Centralized plans**: Domes and rotundas emphasizing vertical unity rather than longitudinal procession
- **Rational clarity**: Elimination of Medieval complexity; emphasis on legible structure
- **Integration of theory and practice**: Architects as learned designers, not mere builders

## Key Terms

- **Dome**: A hemispherical or near-hemispherical vault; Renaissance version often uses double shells and Classical proportions
- **Double-shell dome**: Two concentric domes with internal ribbing and space between, as in Brunelleschi's Florence Cathedral dome
- **Classical orders**: Systematic column types—Doric (sturdy), Ionic (graceful), Corinthian (ornate)—derived from Roman architecture
- **Entablature**: The horizontal structure above columns, consisting of architrave, frieze, and cornice
- **Harmonic proportion**: Proportional relationships derived from musical intervals (ratios like 2:3, 3:4)
- **Centralized plan**: A church or building organized around a central vertical axis (dome or rotunda) rather than longitudinal procession
- **Greek cross**: A cross with four equal arms; often used in centralized Renaissance churches
- **Pediment**: A triangular gable above a portico or facade, derived from Classical temples
- **Portico**: A covered entrance or porch with columns, derived from Classical temple design
- **Mannerism**: A late Renaissance style emphasizing tension, distortion of Classical rules, and dramatic effects (Michelangelo's later work)

## Learning Goal

By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define a masonry unit and distinguish between concrete blocks, clay bricks, and stone
- Identify CHB (concrete hollow block) standard dimensions and grades
- Explain the role of mortar in bonding units and accommodating movement
- Describe the difference between load-bearing and non-load-bearing masonry units

---
Masonry units are classified as hollow or solid based on the ratio of void area to gross cross-sectional area. Understanding these classifications, area definitions (gross, net, bedded), and how they affect design and construction is critical for specifying materials, calculating masonry strength, and meeting code requirements.

## Core Concept
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="ArticleMedia" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: id="media-lea-strc-010-02-core-concept", type="image", caption="Masonry Unit Types — Concrete Block, Clay Brick, and Structural Clay Tile", description="Comparative illustration of masonry units: (1) Concrete masonry unit (CMU) — hollow and solid types, nominal sizes (4'', 6'', 8''), web/shell thickness; (2) Clay brick — modular (8×4×2.67''), Norman, Roman, Jumbo sizes; (3) Structural clay tile — load-bearing partition and floor tiles. Compressive strength grades per ASTM/NSCP shown for each unit type.", suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image", status="placeholder"
- Text: (none detected)
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

A **masonry unit** is an individual element (brick, concrete block, stone) used to construct masonry walls. The internal structure—whether the unit contains voids (hollow) or is completely solid—determines its classification and structural behavior.

**Hollow masonry units** contain enclosed voids or cells. The classification threshold is determined by comparing net area (solid material area) to gross cross-sectional area (the total bounding envelope). A masonry unit is classified as **hollow** if its net area is _less than_ 75% of the gross cross-sectional area. Conversely, a unit is classified as **solid** if its net area is _greater than or equal to_ 75% of the gross area.

**Gross area** is the overall cross-sectional area of the unit as measured at the bed face (the face that contacts mortar). It is the total bounding rectangle, including voids.

**Net area** is the cross-sectional area of solid material only, excluding all voids. Net area is determined by subtracting the area of all cells, cores, or holes from the gross area.

**Bedded area** (sometimes called bedding area or contact area) is the area of the unit that actually contacts mortar in the bed joint. For concrete hollow blocks with cells running perpendicular to the bed joint, the bedded area is typically 50–60% of the gross area (only the solid "shells" of the unit contact mortar). This distinction is essential in grouted masonry design because grout in cells does not develop the same bond strength as solid masonry.

### Concrete Hollow Block (CHB) Standard Dimensions

Concrete hollow blocks are the dominant masonry unit in the Philippines. Standard sizes include:

| _Designation_ | _Thickness (D)_ | _Height (H)_ | _Length (L)_ | _Typical Cell Count_ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4-inch CHB | 100 mm | 200 mm | 400 mm | 2–3 cells |
| 5-inch CHB | 125 mm | 200 mm | 400 mm | 2–3 cells |
| 6-inch CHB | 150 mm | 200 mm | 400 mm | 2–3 cells |

A standard 6-inch CHB with gross area = 0.150 m × 0.400 m = 0.060 m² and typical net area ≈ 0.030 m² (50%) is classified as **hollow** because 0.030 ÷ 0.060 = 50% < 75%.

### Design Implications

In **unreinforced masonry**, hollow units transfer compressive loads through the solid material (webs and shells); the hollow cells provide no structural contribution. In **grouted reinforced masonry**, grout fills designated cells, enabling vertical reinforcement to transfer load and providing confinement. However, grouted cells do not develop the same lateral bond strength as solid material; this is accounted for in allowable stress calculations.

The **bedded area** concept is critical: the bearing strength of masonry (compression perpendicular to the bed joint) is calculated as stress = load ÷ bedded area, not gross area. Because bedded area of hollow units is much smaller than gross area (typically 50–60%), the bearing stress is proportionally higher, and local crushing is a common failure mode in masonry.

## Key Provisions

| _Unit Classification_ | _Net Area / Gross Area_ | _Cell Void Condition_ | _Structural Behavior_ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hollow | < 75% | Enclosed voids; may be empty or grouted | Load transfers through solid shells; grouted cells confine reinforcement |
| Solid | ≥ 75% | Minimal voids or solid throughout | Load transfers uniformly through unit; higher bearing capacity |

| _Area Type_ | _Definition_ | _Used In_ | _Example (6-inch CHB)_ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross area | Total bounding cross-section, including all voids | Calculating unit dimensions, initial specifications | 150 mm × 400 mm = 60,000 mm² |
| Net area | Solid material only; voids excluded | Classifying unit as hollow or solid (75% threshold) | 30,000 mm² (50% of gross = hollow) |
| Bedded area | Area actually contacting mortar in bed joint | Calculating bearing stress, lateral bond strength | 30,000–36,000 mm² (50–60% of gross) |

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, concrete hollow blocks (CHB) are the standard unit for masonry construction, with net-to-gross ratios typically 45–55% (solidly in the hollow classification). The BCP (Building Code of the Philippines, now incorporated into the NBP 2020) recognizes hollow units and specifies grouting schedules and reinforcement placement accordingly. Structural designers must account for bedded area when calculating bearing stresses and ensuring local crushing does not occur. The widespread use of 6-inch CHB reflects the balance between cost, availability, and structural adequacy for typical residential and low-rise commercial construction.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1 — Classification Threshold:**
_A concrete block has a gross area of 150,000 mm² and a net area of 105,000 mm². Is this unit classified as hollow or solid?_
- Correct answer: Solid. Net area ÷ gross area = 105,000 ÷ 150,000 = 70% > 75%? No, 70% < 75%, so the unit is hollow. (Recheck: 105,000 / 150,000 = 0.70 = 70%, which is less than 75%, so HOLLOW.)
- Test variation: Apply the threshold to hypothetical units with varying void percentages.

**Pattern 2 — Bedded Area Application:**
_A 150 mm thick concrete hollow block wall carries a factored axial load of 300 kN per unit width. The bedded area is 55% of the gross area (150 mm × 400 mm). Calculate the bearing stress and determine if the unit is adequate if the design bearing strength is 5 MPa._
- Correct answer: Gross area = 0.150 × 0.400 = 0.060 m² per meter of wall; bedded area = 0.055 × 0.060 = 0.033 m² per unit; bearing stress = 300 kN ÷ 0.033 m² = 9.1 MPa > 5 MPa (INADEQUATE—local crushing risk).
- Test variation: Vary load, bedded area percentage, and allowable stress.

**Pattern 3 — Grouting Strategy in Hollow Units:**
_In a four-story hollow CHB building with Design Category D seismic loading, grouted cells are specified at 1200 mm intervals horizontally and in all courses at specified vertical reinforcement locations. Why is full grouting of all cells not required?_
- Correct answer: Full grouting is economically wasteful and structurally unnecessary; strategic grouting around reinforcement and at specified intervals provides required lateral confinement and vertical load paths at lower cost. Ungrouted cells maintain thermal insulation value.
- Test variation: Recognize the balance between structural performance and constructability.

## Learning Goal
Apply landscape design principles — landform, plant composition, water features, hardscape materials — to create functional outdoor spaces, design planting plans for Philippine tropical conditions, and integrate landscape with site drainage and circulation.

Landscape design transforms outdoor spaces through the strategic integration of natural (softscape) and built (hardscape) elements. Mastering landscape principles requires understanding how landforms, plants, water, and human-made features work together to create functional, beautiful, and resilient environments. 
### Landscape Design Fundamentals

Landscape design is the profession and practice of designing outdoor spaces—parks, gardens, streetscapes, campuses, and larger land areas. Unlike architecture, which focuses on buildings, landscape design shapes the land itself and manages the relationship between the built and natural environments. In the Philippines, landscape design responds to tropical climate, diverse ecosystems, and the need for water-efficient design.

**Key distinction:** Landscape design differs from landscape architecture. Landscape design is the conceptual and aesthetic process; landscape architecture is the licensed profession regulated under the scope of practice for architects.

### Hardscape and Softscape Components

Landscape spaces are composed of two fundamental categories:

**Hardscape** consists of permanent, built structures and surfaces:
- Paving materials (concrete, asphalt, pavers, permeable surfaces)
- Walls and fences
- Water features (fountains, ponds, channels)
- Lighting
- Seating and furniture
- Structures (pergolas, pavilions, bridges)

Hardscape provides durability, defines spatial boundaries, and supports program activities.

**Softscape** consists of living and natural elements:
- Turf and groundcovers
- Trees and shrubs
- Herbaceous plants (flowers, perennials)
- Soil and mulch
- Water bodies and wetlands

Softscape provides ecological function, seasonal change, shade, and habitat.

A successful landscape balances hardscape and softscape. Too much hardscape creates hostile, heat-absorbing environments; too much softscape without structure lacks definition and clarity.

### Site Grading and Drainage Fundamentals

Site grading is the process of reshaping the land to establish proper drainage, create level areas for use, and respond to existing topography. Proper grading is essential for site health and safety.

**Key grading principles:**

1. **Surface drainage:** Water must drain away from buildings and activity areas. Grade minimum 2% slope away from structures to prevent water damage.

2. **Drainage swleas and bioretention:** Depressed, vegetated areas collect and filter stormwater runoff. These reduce flooding, improve water infiltration, and recharge groundwater.

3. **Terracing and retaining walls:** On sloped sites, terracing creates level platforms for buildings or plazas. Retaining walls hold soil on slopes.

### Planting Design Principles

Planting design selects plant species and arranges them to achieve functional and aesthetic goals.

**Key planting design concepts:**

**Massing and composition** — Groups of plants create visual rhythm and enclosure. Single plants appear weak; massed plantings of the same species (minimum three of a kind) create visual impact. Odd numbers (3, 5, 7) are more visually dynamic than even groups.

**Layering** — Plant communities have horizontal layers: canopy trees (tallest), understory trees, shrubs, groundcovers, and herbaceous perennials. Layering mimics natural forest structure, increases habitat diversity, and creates visual depth.

**Seasonal interest** — Thoughtful plant selection ensures visual interest year-round through flowering times, foliage color changes, fruit, and winter structure.

**Texture and form** — Plant foliage texture (fine, medium, bold) and branching form (columnar, spreading, weeping) vary spatial experience and visual contrast.

**Maintenance intensity** — Plant selection must match the site's maintenance capacity. Heavily manicured planting requires skilled pruning; naturalistic planting tolerates more variation.

### Xeriscaping and Water-Efficient Landscape Design

Xeriscaping is landscape design that minimizes water use through plant selection and efficient irrigation management. The prefix "xero-" means dry. Xeriscaping is not about creating dry, barren landscapes—it is about creating beautiful landscapes that use water efficiently by choosing appropriate plants and design strategies.

**Core xeriscaping principles:**

1. **Native and adapted species:** Drought-tolerant native plants survive with natural rainfall and need no supplemental watering once established. Native species are ecologically beneficial, requiring no fertilizers or pesticides.

2. **Appropriate plant grouping (hydrozoning):** Group plants by water needs. High-water plants (near permanent irrigation) are clustered separately from drought-tolerant plants that need minimal watering. This avoids over-watering drought-tolerant species.

3. **Soil improvement:** High-quality soil with organic matter retains more water. Mulch (wood chips, bark) over soil reduces evaporation by 50% or more.

4. **Efficient irrigation:** Drip irrigation delivers water directly to plant roots, eliminating waste from sprinkler overspray. Drip systems reduce water use by 30–50% compared to spray irrigation.

5. **Reduced turf areas:** Turf grass is water-intensive. Replacing some turf with native groundcovers, hardscape, or meadow reduces irrigation demand.

6. **Permeable surfaces:** Permeable pavement (permeable pavers, porous asphalt) allows water to infiltrate into soil rather than running off, reducing flooding and recharging groundwater.

**Philippine application:** In the Philippines, xeriscaping using native, drought-tolerant species is increasingly important for resilience to climate variability and water scarcity. Cities adopting water-efficient design reduce stormwater flooding and municipal water demand.

## Learning Goal
Apply sustainable urban development principles — compact, mixed-use, transit-oriented, walkable neighborhoods — design Complete Streets for Philippine conditions, and align planning with SDG 11 and New Urban Agenda frameworks.

Sustainable urban development integrates environmental, social, and economic goals through compact, mixed-use neighborhoods supported by transit and walkable streets. Complete Streets design moves beyond car-centric infrastructure to create pedestrian, bicycle, and transit-friendly public spaces. Together, they form a planning approach aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities) and the New Urban Agenda from Habitat III (2016).

## Core Concept

Sustainable urban development pursues three objectives simultaneously: (1) minimizing environmental impact through compact, efficient land use; (2) ensuring equitable access to housing, jobs, and services; and (3) supporting long-term economic vitality. Rather than sprawling, car-dependent growth, sustainable development concentrates mixed-use neighborhoods—residential, commercial, office, cultural—within walkable distances, served by efficient public transit.

Key frameworks include:

1. **New Urbanism** (1980s–present) — walkable neighborhoods with mixed uses, human-scale architecture, and transit connectivity. The traditional 5-minute walk radius of 400 meters enables pedestrian-based daily errands.

2. **Transit-Oriented Development (TOD)** — higher-density, mixed-use development within 400–800 meters of transit stations, encouraging mode shift from private vehicles to public transit.

3. **15-Minute City** (Carlos Moreno, Paris 2020) — urban design ensuring that all daily essentials—work, education, healthcare, shopping, culture, leisure—are accessible within 15 minutes of walk or bicycle ride from home.

4. **Smart Growth** — compact development, infill, mixed uses, walkability, transit choice, environmental preservation, and community participation.

5. **Complete Streets** — street design that accommodates pedestrians, cyclists, transit users, and drivers; prioritizes safety and livability over vehicle throughput alone.

These frameworks share a common critique of 20th-century car-dependent suburban sprawl and a commitment to human-scale, livable urban forms. In Philippine context, Complete Streets addresses the reality that most Filipinos walk or use transit; car-centric design ignores the majority.

## Philippine Context

Philippine cities face the tension between rapid growth and livability. Metro Manila's sprawl, traffic congestion, and pollution exemplify car-dependent development that benefits car owners while marginalizing pedestrians and transit users (the majority). Complete Streets design in Philippine cities means prioritizing sidewalk width, shade, accessibility for persons with disabilities, and safe crossing rather than maximizing vehicle lanes. New Urbanism and 15-Minute City concepts address the reality that middle- and low-income Filipinos depend on walking and public transit. Sustainability frameworks in Philippine CLUPs increasingly emphasize mixed-use zoning, TOD around transit stations, and pedestrian infrastructure as alternatives to sprawl-driven congestion.

## How It's Tested

1. **Framework definition and application** — "Which planning approach emphasizes that all daily needs should be accessible within a 15-minute walk from home?" → Answer: 15-Minute City (Carlos Moreno). Tests concept recall and context.

2. **Complete Streets in Philippine context** — "A municipal engineer proposes widening a street by reducing sidewalk width. Does this align with Complete Streets design?" → Answer: No; Complete Streets prioritizes pedestrian safety and comfort, especially in contexts where walking is the primary mode. This tests understanding of Complete Streets principles applied to low-car-dependency contexts.

3. **TOD catchment and zoning** — "A new MRT station is being planned in a residential area. What density and mix of uses should planning allow within the TOD walkable catchment (400–800m)?" → Answer: Higher density, mixed-use development (residential + commercial + office) to support transit ridership and reduce car dependency. Tests application of TOD principles to specific development scenarios.

## Learning Goal

Identify the four regional traditions of American colonial architecture — New England (timber, chimney, saltbox), Mid-Atlantic (brick, symmetry, Georgian), Dutch (gambrel roof, stone), Spanish/Southwest (coquina, adobe, mission) — by material, climate, and cultural origin.
## Core Concept

American colonial architecture was not a monolith. Regional climate, available materials, cultural origin, and economic systems produced distinct building traditions across thirteen colonies. New England built timber-frame houses with central chimneys and steep roofs (shedding snow). The Chesapeake region built brick plantation houses with symmetrical facades (classical ideals, labor-intensive). Dutch New York left steep-roofed townhouses. Spanish Florida used coquina and thick walls. This diversity reflects colonial reality: each region had different settlers, different resources, different ambitions.

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Colonial builders followed vernacular traditions and European precedent filtered through practical constraints. A New England meetinghouse was not a cathedral—it was a timber box with a gallery for additional seating, reflecting both Puritan theology (simple worship) and economic reality (timber was abundant, stone was not). A Virginia plantation house was a calculated statement of class: symmetrical facades expressed enlightenment order and European refinement, while the dependency buildings (kitchens, slave quarters, storehouses) remained invisible at a distance.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Note" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: Plantation house architecture is inseparable from the enslaved labor that built it and enabled its wealth. The symmetrical facade, classical refinement, and spatial hierarchy all express a system of forced labor and racial hierarchy—do not discuss plantation houses without explicitly addressing slavery.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

The **Federal period** (1780–1820) marked the transition from colonial dependency to American nationhood. Architects and educated patrons embraced **neoclassicism**—the style of republican Rome and Enlightenment reason. **Robert Adam** and English neoclassical precedent influenced American designers. The first American-born architects (Benjamin Latrobe, Charles Bulfinch) synthesized classical proportion with American practicality. Federal-style houses retained colonial proportions but refined details: elliptical windows, delicate ornament, attenuated forms. Civic buildings became temples: courthouses and statehouse faced in stone or brick with porticos proclaiming democratic virtue.

- Text: Do not treat Federal style as simply imported English neoclassicism. Federal is hybrid—classical language (portico, column, proportion) filtered through American democratic ideology and practical constraints (budget, local materials, climate). It is transformation, not mere copy.

## Key Terms

**Timber-Frame Construction** — Structural system using heavy wooden posts, beams, and braces jointed together; primary building method in colonial New England and Mid-Atlantic.

**Central Chimney** — Masonry stack serving multiple fireplaces; positioned in center of colonial house for structural stability and heat distribution.

**Symmetrical Facade** — Balanced arrangement of windows and doors around central entrance; reflects Enlightenment classical ideals; standard in colonial and Federal civic and domestic architecture.

**Neoclassicism** — Architectural revival of classical Greek and Roman forms; emerged in 18th-century Europe and adopted by American Federal architects as symbol of democratic republic.

**Portico** — Covered entrance with columns and pediment; classical element applied to Federal houses and civic buildings.

**Pilaster** — Flattened column attached to wall; classical detail; common on Federal-style facades.

**Meetinghouse** — New England Protestant gathering space; timber-frame, gallery, simple interior; reflects Puritan theology and regional resources.

**Plantation House** — Large domestic structure on agricultural estate; symmetrical, formal; supported by enslaved labor and economic hierarchy.

The Inca mastered exactly this problem — terraced stone platforms stabilizing Andean slopes up to 45 degrees, with integrated drainage and walls engineered to flex during seismic events — all without mortar, iron tools, or the wheel.

## Core Concepts and Memory Aid

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Memory Aid: "I-S-M = Inca Stone Magic."** Three principles: Interlocking (ashlar masonry with trapezoidal joints — no mortar needed), Shaping (stones shaped by hammering/pecking, not cutting — the "Inca puzzle"), S (Seismic resilience — trapezoidal doors/windows and battered walls distribute earthquake forces). All three translate directly to Philippine seismic design principles.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Memory Aid — "A-T-E" (Ashlar, Terracing, Engineering)** Think: *"Andes Tamed Everything"* — the Inca turned the most hostile terrain on earth into a functioning empire.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

- **Ashlar Masonry:** Precisely cut polygonal stone blocks fitted dry (without mortar), relying on friction and interlocking geometry for stability. The finest examples use andesite and granite blocks weighing over 100 tonnes, dressed using harder hammer stones (no iron tools existed in pre-Columbian South America). Walls employ a trapezoidal batter — wider at the base, tapering inward — which lowers the center of gravity and allows controlled movement during earthquakes.
- **Terracing (*Andenes*):** Stepped agricultural and urban platforms carved into mountain slopes. Stone retaining walls hold back fill layers of gravel (drainage), sand (filtration), and topsoil. Integrated channels and aqueducts manage water flow, preventing erosion and landslides. The Inca transformed millions of hectares of otherwise unusable Andean terrain into productive land.
- **Engineering Marvels:** The Qhapaq Ñan road network extended over 30,000 km (UNESCO figure; some estimates reach 40,000 km), connecting the empire from modern Colombia to Argentina across deserts, rainforests, and mountain passes above 6,000 m elevation. Hydraulic engineering at sites like Tipón demonstrates aqueducts with precisely calibrated 1–2% gradients for self-cleaning water flow.

## Active Recall Questions

**Question 1.** What is the primary seismic adaptation of Inca ashlar masonry walls?

A. Reinforced concrete cores hidden within decorative stone cladding  
B. Lime mortar joints that absorb lateral movement through plastic deformation  
C. Trapezoidal batter profile (inward lean) with mortarless friction-fit joints that allow micro-movement during earthquakes  
D. Timber post-and-beam framing concealed behind stone veneer walls  

> **Correct Answer: C.** The Inca's trapezoidal batter (walls wider at the base and leaning inward) lowers the center of gravity, while the mortarless friction-fit joints permit individual stones to shift slightly during seismic events and resettle afterward without structural failure. This is analogous to modern seismic isolation principles. No mortar, concrete, or hidden framing was used.

**Question 2.** The Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, extended approximately how far?

A. 5,000 km, connecting Cusco to Lima along the coast  
B. 30,000 km or more, connecting six modern South American nations from Colombia to Argentina  
C. 12,000 km, limited to the highland plateau between Peru and Bolivia  
D. 80,000 km, spanning both North and South America  

> **Correct Answer: B.** UNESCO describes the Qhapaq Ñan as covering more than 30,000 km (some scholarly estimates reach 40,000 km). It connected the Inca Empire across six modern nations — Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina — traversing coastal deserts, Andean peaks above 6,000 m, and Amazon rainforest. It remains the most extensive pre-Columbian road system in the Americas.

**Question 3.** Which of the following best describes the layered composition of Inca agricultural terraces (*andenes*)?

A. Rammed earth walls with timber reinforcement and a single soil layer  
B. Dry-stone retaining walls with layered fill — large gravel at the bottom for drainage, sand for filtration, and topsoil on the surface  
C. Mortared rubble-core walls with clay waterproofing and volcanic ash soil  
D. Adobe brick retaining walls with straw-reinforced planting beds  

> **Correct Answer: B.** Inca *andenes* used dry-stone retaining walls backed by a carefully engineered fill sequence: coarse gravel at the bottom (rapid drainage), sand in the middle (filtration), and fertile topsoil on top (planting medium). This layered system prevents waterlogging, controls erosion, and sustains agriculture on extreme slopes — a principle directly applicable to modern hillside development in the Philippine Cordillera.

---



---

## Exam Tip

ALE Trap: Three Inca features: (1) Ashlar polygonal masonry = stones cut to fit WITHOUT mortar, earthquake-resistant through friction, (2) Trapezoidal openings = doors, windows, niches all trapezoidal, (3) Kancha = standardized rectangular enclosure plan. Machu Picchu is the most tested Inca site. The mortarless ashlar masonry is the defining feature — NO other civilization used this technique at this scale.
